title: Desktop apps
content: Desktop Apps Run your WebUI templates in a native window using WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS, or GTK4/WebKitGTK 6 on Linux. Source and bundled apps render through Rust without shipping Node or a browser engine. An optional Rust host can instead show an existing loopback HTTP application. The target machine still needs the platform's webview and runtime prerequisites. Get started For a JavaScript project, opt in to desktop support with matching package versions: npm pnpm Yarn Bun npm in

title: Hydration
content: Hydration Hydration attaches browser bindings and listeners to existing server-rendered HTML. Import your authored component modules from a browser entry to register them; static SSR does not require the framework. Component files Browser behavior user-card.html + user-card.ts or user-card.js The authored class owns events, lifecycle, reactive state, and imperative APIs user-card.html only The server-rendered HTML stays inactive unless later navigation or state changes require browser rendering

title: Language integrations
content: Language Integrations Compile templates with webui build , then render the resulting protocol.bin through the binding for your backend. The renderer is Rust; it does not require a JavaScript SSR engine. Your host supplies state, HTTP responses, and asset delivery. content: .NET The Microsoft.WebUI NuGet package wraps the Rust renderer's C ABI with safe handles and managed result types. It targets .NET 8 and .NET 9 and restores matching native runtime packages. Load one Protocol for repeated renders, then dispose native-backed objects when their work is complete. Installation Check package availability first. title: C API and FFI
content: C API Build WebUI as a native shared library to call the Rust renderer through C interop. Load a protocol handle once, reuse it for rendering, and release each result with its designated function. Your host must support the target's native library and ABI; this does not require a JavaScript SSR engine. Prefer the official Go module , managed Microsoft.WebUI package , or native Python package for those languages. Direct FFI and ctypes examples below illustrate the lower-level ownership contract.

title: Go
content: Go The github.com/microsoft/webui/go/v3 module renders through WebUI's native Rust C ABI. It has no third-party Go dependencies and does not run JavaScript to render HTML. The package owns native handles; your application owns HTTP, request state, and public asset delivery. Installation You need Go 1.25 or newer, cgo, a compatible C compiler, and the WebUI native SDK matching webui.Version , your operating system, and architecture. go get github.com/microsoft/webui/go/v3 Tagged Go module version

title: Node.js and Bun
content: Node.js and Bun @microsoft/webui exposes the Rust renderer through a platform-specific native addon for Node.js and Bun. Load protocol.bin once, reuse the Protocol , and pass JSON state for each render. Buffered output is a UTF-8 Buffer . Installation npm pnpm Yarn Bun npm install @microsoft/webui pnpm add @microsoft/webui yarn add @microsoft/webui bun add @microsoft/webui Keep optional dependencies enabled so your manager can install the matching native package. title: Python
content: Python The microsoft-webui package is a native PyO3 binding, imported as microsoft_webui . Reuse a Renderer to render compiled protocols with request-specific state. Calls release the GIL but remain synchronous on the calling thread; ASGI hosts should offload them. Installation The microsoft-webui package is not published to PyPI yet . title: Rust
content: Rust The microsoft-webui crate, imported as webui , provides build and rendering APIs. Load one Protocol at startup and reuse it with request state. WebUIHandler writes HTML through ResponseWriter ; the host chooses buffered output or a backpressured streaming writer. Custom writers only need to implement write and end . Cache tags, pending UI, and error components are optional route attributes validated at build time. Their browser behavior runs in the router, not in the server's JavaScript engine. Add a same-named .ts or .js file only when the component needs interactive behavior . Component Discovery WebUI sc

title: CSS tokens and themes
content: CSS Tokens and Themes Style components with ordinary CSS custom properties. You can define them in your own stylesheets, or use --theme to validate and supply a shared token set. Theming does not scope selectors: Light DOM CSS is global in its owning CSS tree; Shadow DOM provides native isolation. /* my-card.css, using the default Shadow DOM mode */ :host { color : var( -- text-primary ); background : var( -- surface-page ); } Configure a theme Theme files map token names without -- to CSS value

title: Attribute and property bindings
content: Attribute Directives Use an ordinary binding for an attribute value, ? for conditional presence, or : to pass a value to a child DOM property. Simple Dynamic Attributes Use {{}} inside an attribute value to bind it to a state value: < a href = " {{url}} " >{{linkText}}</ a > < img src = " {{imageUrl}} " alt = " {{imageAlt}} " /> Example State: { " url " : "https://example.com", " linkText " : "Visit Example" } Output: < a href = " https://example.com " >Visit Example</ a > A whole-binding attrib

title: Streaming boundaries
content: Streaming Boundaries <boundary> marks a complete region that WebUI can render, flush, and hydrate before the rest of the response arrives. It is a compile-time directive and does not create a DOM wrapper. Use it with a host's progressive streaming API and the browser streaming coordinator; adding the directive alone does not turn an ordinary render into a progressively hydrated response. title: Lists and loops
content: <for> Loop Directive Use <for each="item in items"> to repeat HTML for each array item. The directive itself adds no DOM wrapper. Basic Usage < for each = " item in items " > < div class = " item " > < h3 >{{item.title}}</ h3 > < p >{{item.description}}</ p > </ div > </ for > Each iteration binds item to the current value. Missing or empty arrays render no items. For lists that reorder, use explicit keys to keep DOM and component state attached to the same item. Using the Loop Variable The loop

title: Conditional rendering
content: <if> Conditional Directive Use <if condition="..."> to include a region when its condition is truthy. The directive does not create an extra DOM element. Its attributes are condition and optional lazy , whose value is an optional prefetch trigger. Unsupported attributes, including id , are build errors. title: Deferred rendering and hydration
content: Lazy Component Policy Defer offscreen browser work with attributes on a component's root <template> . Rendering and hydration are separate: rendering is layout and paint; hydration attaches bindings and listeners. Hydration explains lifecycle behavior, while Performance explains when deferral is worthwhile. title: Text and raw HTML bindings
content: Text Bindings Insert state with {{path}} . Use triple braces only for trusted HTML. These bindings read values; they do not evaluate arbitrary JavaScript, call functions, or perform arithmetic. Escaped Signals: {{}} The double curly braces syntax ( {{}} ) inserts a value from the state object with HTML escaping applied: < p >Hello, {{user.name}}!</ p > HTML characters in the value are escaped so they display as text rather than markup. title: How It Works
content: How It Works WebUI separates the files you author from the work each request and browser must do. The important boundary is simple: the server renders templates with data, not by running your component TypeScript. The diagram describes responsibilities, not measured timings. In a normal SSR deployment, protocol.bin stays on the server. The browser receives HTML and the assets needed by the page. title: Interactivity

Its HTML and CSS stay in paired files; the optional @microsoft/webui-framework runtime connects that behavior to server-rendered content. WebUI uses Trusted Types automatically for compiled templates. Applications control enforcement through CSP; raw state HTML is not promoted through the compiler policy. content: Coming from React You already know the useful ideas: describe UI from state, compose components, pass data down, and handle user intent. WebUI keeps those ideas, but puts structure in HTML templates, styling in CSS, and browser behavior in TypeScript. Both systems are declarative. title: Why WebUI?
content: Why WebUI? Choose WebUI when you want server-rendered HTML from a native backend and explicit control over the browser code your application loads. It combines a compiled template format, a Rust renderer, and optional Web Component behavior. Origin WebUI started inside Microsoft Edge, where UI needed to fit a native Chromium host rather than require a separate JavaScript rendering service. title: What is WebUI?
content: What is WebUI? WebUI builds web apps from HTML templates, CSS, and data. A compiler prepares the templates before requests arrive. A native renderer fills them with your backend's data to produce HTML. Add TypeScript where a component needs browser behavior, such as responding to a button. Start here These lessons assume you can edit HTML and run commands in a terminal. Installation and the first three lessons use one hello-webui project.
